questions.question:
Refer to the CORS preflight request flow below. Why does the browser send an OPTIONS request before the actual POST?

Browser → OPTIONS /api/data (preflight) → Server → Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * → Browser → POST /api/data (actual request) → Server → 200 OK

values: Step 1: Browser detects cross-origin POST with custom headers
Step 2: Browser sends OPTIONS /api/data with Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
Step 3: Server responds with CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin, etc.)
Step 4: If preflight passes, browser sends actual POST request
Step 5: Server responds 200 OK with data

options: OPTIONS is sent because POST requests are not supported for cross-origin requests
The browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request to check if the server allows the actual cross-origin request before sending it
OPTIONS is an optimisation — it caches the CORS headers to avoid re-sending them
The server forces OPTIONS before POST for all requests, not just cross-origin
questions.answer: The browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request to check if the server allows the actual cross-origin request before sending it

questions.question:
Scenario:
A developer builds a REST API. They use HTTP 200 for all responses including errors, returning { error: 'Not Found' } in the body for missing resources. Why is this considered a bad practice?
options: HTTP 200 with an error body is faster than using proper status codes
It violates REST semantics — clients and intermediaries (caches, proxies) rely on HTTP status codes to understand response meaning; 200 tells them the request succeeded even when it failed
HTTP 200 cannot carry a JSON body with an error field
Only 5xx codes should be used for all errors in REST APIs
questions.answer: It violates REST semantics — clients and intermediaries (caches, proxies) rely on HTTP status codes to understand response meaning; 200 tells them the request succeeded even when it failed

questions.question: What is the primary difference between a GET and POST request in terms of data transmission and caching?
options: GET sends data in the URL query string and can be cached; POST sends data in the request body and is not cached by default
GET is encrypted; POST is plain text
POST can handle larger payloads because it uses chunked encoding; GET is limited to 100 bytes
GET and POST are identical — the difference is only in the method name used
questions.answer: GET sends data in the URL query string and can be cached; POST sends data in the request body and is not cached by default

Browser sends a new request — 3600 seconds = 60 minutes; the cache has expired at 11:00 AM
Browser sends a conditional request — must-revalidate forces a server check every time
Browser blocks the second request — must-revalidate prevents duplicate fetches
questions.answer: Browser sends a new request — 3600 seconds = 60 minutes; the cache has expired at 11:00 AM

questions.question: What does the Domain Name System (DNS) resolve, and at which step does it occur in a typical browser page load?

A React parent passes a function prop to a child. The child re-renders every time the parent renders, even when the function has not changed. Which hook prevents unnecessary re-renders of the child?

options: useRef — stores the function reference without causing re-renders

useState — stores the function in state so it does not change on render
questions.answer: useCallback — memoises the function reference so the same reference is passed to the child unless dependencies change

options: React → Redux → Axios → Express → MongoDB → Express → Axios → Redux → React
React → Express → Redux → MongoDB → Axios → React
Redux → React → MongoDB → Express → Axios
React → Axios → MongoDB → Express → Redux → React
